title: There is a Light That Never Goes Out

cards.headline: Marr's in-joke chord riff, borrowed from the Stones
cards.snippet: In 1993, Johnny Marr explained that the ascending F♯m–A–B chord sequence in the Smiths' song came from the Rolling Stones' cover of Marvin Gaye's "Hitch Hike". He said he included it as an "in-joke", to see whether the music press would credit the Velvet Underground's "There She Goes Again" as the inspiration. Marr contended the Velvet Underground had "stole" the figure from "Hitch Hike" themselves. He said he knew he was smarter than that, because he was listening to what the Velvet Underground were listening to.

cards.headline: Those strings are an Emulator, not an orchestra
cards.snippet: In late 1985, the Smiths recorded this song at London's RAK Studios, with a synthesised string arrangement that Johnny Marr built on an E-mu Emulator. Morrissey was sceptical about fake strings. But the band had no budget for a real ensemble and didn't want outsiders in the process, so he changed his mind. The album credits the strings to the "Hated Salford Ensemble". The recording was completed in November at Jacobs Studios in Farnham, Surrey.
cards.context: Recorded in late 1985, with the recording completed at Jacobs Studios in Farnham.

cards.headline: A death wish phrased as the sweetest thing you could say to someone
cards.snippet: Per the Genius annotation, Morrissey turns depression and suicidal thoughts into a romantic fantasy, wishing to die in a moment of joy. It may also read as unrequited love: he'd rather die beside this person than confess.
cards.context: One commenter calls it "The saddest compliment" (22,000 likes). Another hopes to be "by the love of my life" when they die.
